Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

Taiming Lu  Sachin Konan  Zhuang Liu
Princeton University
ai-scientist.world

Abstract

  • AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted — centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper’s open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (↑\uparrow158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists’ own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.

§ 1 Introduction

A new kind of scientist has arrived — for the first time, an intelligence advances the very thing it is made of.
AI-Scientists are the first whose discoveries improve the discoverer (Boiko et al., 2023; Gottweis et al., 2025; Mitchener et al., 2025). They now invent new AI on their own (Yamada et al., 2025; Schmidgall et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026). This could set off a chain reaction, and every gain makes the next one faster (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). This is the power of a scientist, the power of research.

What is research? It is not a single ability, and it is not a single task. Watch a scientist at work: they read until they find something no one has explained, guess at the reason, and build an experiment to test it. It fails. They eventually figure out what the failure is telling them, adjust, and run it again. It works. Next month they are doing the same on a different problem, in a different part of the field. What makes them a scientist is not any one of these moves; it is the judgment that runs through all of them, and carries from one problem to the next. That is why research cannot live in a single task. Nailing one problem is a trick; research is the ability to discover again and again, problem after problem. We believe the same for a scientist of AI.

A scientist like that keeps growing, and it needs a world big enough to grow in. Human researchers already live in such a world: the scientific literature. It provides two things. The first is problem: each paper defines a different research question no single answer can exhaust. The second is idea: each paper contributes to the field’s shared memory of approaches, findings, successes, and failures. Together, they drive research as target and foundation. This is the world human scientists have always relied on, and the one AI-Scientists need.

We introduce Scientist World : a living research universe built from the scientific literature itself. In it, each paper becomes an executable scientific environment. We designed a multi-agent pipeline for this conversion, with no human in the loop. There are four steps: (1) reproduce the paper’s method until it recovers the paper’s result; (2) design a research task by defining what counts as scientific progress without shortcuts or gaming; (3) package it so it runs on any machine; and (4) verify it with independent agents. An AI-Scientist is then scored by how much its own method improves over the human researchers’ method, which we call its Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI). Building from high-quality papers, we first release 1,000 environments, and it keeps growing with the literature (Figure 1).

Because the pipeline runs with no human in the loop, Scientist World is Scalable: it can grow fast to cover a broad range of fields and topics. Two more properties are inherited from science itself. Evolving: science never stands still, so a fixed set measures yesterday, what a scientist has already seen; Scientist World absorbs new literature every day, measuring research rather than recall. Execution-grounded: a fluent AI-Scientist can make any idea sound bold, but ideas that impress on paper might fail on execution (Kapoor et al., 2024; Si et al., 2025); because every environment is built and measured through real experiments, research is judged by execution, not rhetoric.

Environments for research exist, but none, to our knowledge, holds the three properties together. Most are not scalable: they recycle problems from past competitions (Huang et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025; Nathani et al., 2025), confine to simulated worlds (Jansen et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b), or hand-pick tasks from a few papers (Wijk et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Garikaparthi et al., 2026). Nearly all are not evolving: sets are fixed at release and age into training data (Sainz et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024), and those that refresh cover only narrower skills such as code (Jain et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). And others are not execution-grounded: they reproduce results the field already knows (Siegel et al., 2024; Starace et al., 2025; Kon et al., 2025) or judge proposed ideas as text (Guo et al., 2025; Si et al., 2025). Scientist World holds three at once (Figure 2).

We first use Scientist World to evaluate frontier AI-Scientists. Each scientist attempts an environment in two modes: improve, which starts from the paper’s idea with its reproduced method; and innovate, which starts from the problem alone. The two abilities prove distinct, since the best improver is not the best inventor. Every attempt leaves a trajectory, each decision paired with the measured outcome of a real experiment, and we release this corpus alongside the environments. Then we train with it: rewarded only by real outcomes, a small scientist learns to propose ideas that, implemented by a fixed frontier executor, reach the frontier cohort’s level on the median held-out environment. Taken together, Scientist World is three things at once:

  • •

    A benchmark. The standing measure of whether AI-Scientists can advance real research.

  • •

    A dataset. A growing corpus of research being done, with every attempt preserved in full loop.

  • •

    A gym. The same environments become training grounds, with real experimental results as rewards.

If research is the ability to discover again and again, it needs a world that never runs out. is that world, grown from science itself and open today. The chain reaction now has a place to happen.

§ 2 From Papers to Environments

How well can AI-Scientists do research? Any answer must come from a research environment: a real problem to work on, and an objective measure of progress. A research paper is almost such an environment. It states a problem, proposes a method, and reports what happened. Yet it is only a record of science done, not a place to do science. We turns the record back into the place. It (1) rebuilds the paper’s idea and experiment, (2) defines what constitutes an improvement, and (3) judges every scientist’s new solution.

We design builder agents to perform this conversion autonomously. They reproduce a paper’s experiment, extract the problem to solve, and design both into a self-contained environment: the problem becomes a task any new scientist can take up, and the reproduced result becomes the bar their solutions are scored against.

2.1 The Builders

We convert each paper through a sequence of agent iterations on one shared workspace (Figure 4). Four roles divide the work, from reproducing the paper to verifying the finished environment. A single paper can take hundreds of unattended turns without a human in the loop. To hold the sequence together, a ladder of milestones is used to track progress. Each rung marks how much of the environment stands, from a first runnable experiment to an environment ready for new scientists. A builder agent ends its iteration by reporting the rung it believes it reached; the next builder begins by checking and verifying that report. At the end of the builder iterations, the final environment is accepted or rejected based on the milestone reported.

Workflow.

A paper moves through builder roles in iterations. Each agent inherits the workspace, audits the claimed milestone, and demotes whatever it cannot support. Every iteration ends at a gate: a milestone below the requirement reverts the work to an earlier iteration, or exits as failure. To be accepted, the experiment must run to support the paper’s central claim. We rotate different builder models across iterations to avoid any blind spots. What survives is a repository that any scientist can use without knowing how it was made.

(1) Reproducer.

The reproducer re-establishes the paper’s main result. It implements both the method and the paper’s original evaluation, from the authors’ code if released or from scratch otherwise. Its experiments scale up from quick checks toward the full run, until the result appears. What it leaves behind we call the source method and the source result: the reproduced method and the numbers it achieved.

(2) Designer.

The designer turns the reproduction into a task that others can attempt. It writes the problem statement that a new scientist will read, and it fixes the rules of the task: which metric to improve, which settings must stay fixed, and which kinds of solution are allowed. It sets the source result as the bar, so a new solution is scored by how much it improves on it. It prepares two evaluation sets: a visible one that the scientist may test against freely, and a held-out one to detect shortcuts or overfitting.

(3) Packager.

The packager makes the designed environment run anywhere, not only on machines that built it. It replaces every local file with a script that downloads it, and declares every dependency the experiments need. The check is simple: a fresh clone of the workspace must be able to rebuild and rerun on its own.

(4) Verifier.

The verifier audits the packaged environment before it is accepted. It rereads the workspace with a skeptic’s eye, checking the code is valid, the scores match the logs, and the task follows the design rules. We keep this role separate on purpose, where the builder that grades the work never built it.

Infrastructure.

All experiments run on a shared pool of compute machines (Figure 5), described in §A with details. A builder never runs jobs on its own hardware: it submits a job, waits, and is woken with the logs when the job ends. We cap each paper’s GPU time a builder can use with a budget enforced outside the builder; when it runs out, the builder wraps up with what it has. With thousands of papers queuing, no single one deserves unbounded compute.

2.2 The Environment

An accepted environment is a paper refactored into an executable research setting. It does not ask a future scientist to reproduce the paper again; it gives that scientist a prepared place to work on the paper’s problem. The repository contains four parts, in the order a scientist encounters them: (1) a task briefing that states the problem, target, allowed direction, and constraints; (2) data and evaluation files that define what a method must produce and how it is scored; (3) the reproduced method and baselines, which provide starting solutions (the source method can optionally be withheld during evaluation); and (4) scripts, score files, logs, job outputs, and commits kept as the construction record. Figure 6 walks through one produced environment in full.

What makes it an environment.

An environment is more than reproduction code. It keeps the paper’s research situation open for new methods. We design each environment around three principles. First, builders may shrink the experiment scale to reduce compute cost, without changing the scientific question. The smaller task should still ask whether the paper’s idea improves the same kind of outcome under the same kind of evaluation. Second, the task must remain non-trivial. The source method should still leave a meaningful gap over simple baselines, so future methods have something real to improve. Third, we treat the reproduced method as one solution, not as the task itself. The data interface and evaluator are written independently of the source method, so a future method can replace it by producing the same kind of artifact.

What makes it a fair task.

We want a future method to win by making progress on the same question, not by changing the question itself. So we write research rules across four files. The problem file states the research question. The target file names what should improve, such as loss or accuracy. The direction file says what kinds of method changes still answer that question. The constraints file lists changes we disallow because they would make the result about a different problem. The constraints also rule out direct scale gains, for example by holding model size, data size, or compute budget fixed when those factors are not the research question.

How a scientist’s attempt is graded.

A scientist’s proposed method is graded on how far it improves over the paper’s source method, on the quantity the claim is about, such as accuracy or loss. This can be viewed as a comparison with human researchers. We score the method over multiple experiments with different metrics used in the original paper. Besides a visible set for development, we reserve a held-out slice, so a method must improve the task rather than exploit one visible number through shortcuts or overfitting (§E.3).

Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI).

We introduce FNI, scored per paper as FNI =100​∑cwc​δc/(σc​b)\text{FNI }=100\sum_{c}w_{c}\,\delta_{c}/(\sigma_{c}b), where δc\delta_{c} is the signed gain over the source method on metric cc, wcw_{c} its weight, σc\sigma_{c} a frozen frontier cohort’s spread on it, and bb sets the cohort’s mean |FNI ||\text{FNI }| to 100; 0 matches the paper, and negative is worse (§E.3).

§ 3 Scientist World

is the artifact built from the environment-construction system: the selected paper set, the generated repositories, and the records produced while building them. This section reports how we choose a valuable, buildable 1,000-paper source set and how the batch conversion ran.

3.1 Building at Scale

Selecting papers.

Our selection pipeline keeps papers that are worth building under budget (Figure 7). We start from arXiv’s core AI categories over fourteen months to obtain 124,816 unique papers. We (1) run two fast screens with MiniMax M2.7 (MiniMax, 2026). The quality screen keeps papers in roughly the top 25% quality band. The type screen keeps empirical-method papers, whose main contribution is quantitative optimization. Together they leave 21,354 papers. Then (2) we run more detailed judgments for each paper on two quantities: research quality and reproduction difficulty (we prefer papers with low compute costs). From the remaining pool, with a geometric-mean utility over quality and feasibility, we sample the category-balanced top 1,000 papers.

Automation.

No human reviews any paper at any stage in our pipeline. The source arXiv categories add roughly 9,000 unique papers per month, of which about 1,500 survive screening and remain feasible. The current 1,000 are the first release; future batches extend the window through the same pipeline.

The build.

We build every paper with the same nine-iteration workflow: three reproducers, three designers, one packager, and two verifier passes (we repeat a role for multiple iterations for additional quality checks), with the model family rotating across GPT, Claude, MiniMax, and GLM. A paper may draw up to 70 GPU-hours, yet the median spends under half of one (Table 1).

3.2 The Built World

Composition.

We first release 1,000 environments spread across eight areas (Figure 8). A scientist therefore meets problems of many kinds, not one narrow family. A typical environment is substantial, closer to a small research project than a single script (Table 2). Because most carry several experiments rather than a single headline result, a later method has multiple quantities to improve rather than one number to chase.

Quality.

Every environment is built without a human in the loop, so we do not take any single builder’s word for its quality. Four checks stand behind an accepted environment, one per row of Table 3:

  • •

    Reproduction fidelity. The reproduced source method’s numbers are checked against the paper’s reported results within a small margin, across every experiment and metric used by the environment; the few exceptions are accepted only with documented justification.

  • •

    Baseline separation. Where a paper provides baselines, we reimplement them and require the reproduced source method to outperform them, preserving a real gap for future methods to close; the rate in Table 3 counts all 1,000 environments, including those without a reimplementable baseline.

  • •

    Iterative cross-checking. Each builder audits the previous milestone claim and demotes whatever the workspace cannot support. A demotion rolls the workflow back to the previous iteration; construction then resumes from that checkpoint until it passes the later checks without further reversion.

  • •

    Independent verification. The final environment must pass a verifier that did not participate in construction. Every released environment satisfies this final check.

Example.

Figure 9 shows one environment end to end. The paper’s question survives intact, whether a transformer can train without normalization, while its experiment shrinks to ImageNet-50 so attempts fit a bounded budget. The constraint is what keeps the task honest: the same model scale, data, and pretraining as the source method, so any gain must come from the method itself. Half of every evaluation stays hidden, so the score reflects what generalizes rather than what was tuned against the visible half.

Openness.

Research rarely hands the scientist an approach. Deciding what to build is much of the work, and a world that always prescribes it would train executors rather than scientists. We therefore judge each task’s materials and place it on a 0 to 100 scale, where 0 means the approach is fully prescribed and 100 means the task fixes only what counts as success and leaves the way there entirely to the scientist. We find that every area covers nearly the whole range (Figure 10): the level of freedom of an environment depends on the task itself, not on where in the world it sits.

§ 4 Scientists in the World

4.1 Benchmark

We now use the environments to evaluate AI-Scientists. Running every model on all 1,000 environments is too costly to repeat, so we evaluate on a fixed cohort of ten lower-compute environments. Each model attempts every environment under the same compute budget, in two modes:

  • •

    Improve mode. The model receives the reproduced source method and tries to improve its result.

  • •

    Innovate mode. The model receives no source code and must design a method from scratch. We ensure there is no leakage of the paper’s original solution.

Each attempt is evaluated on both the visible and held-out splits, with the final FNI score averaged across the two. Zero FNI matches the reproduced source method, while a positive FNI improves on it. Since different environments have different scoring scales, we normalize the scores to aggregate (§E.3).

In the result, the two modes show different strengths across models (Figure 12): Fable 5 is the strongest at improving existing methods, while Fable 5.1 and Fable 5 take the top two places at designing new methods from scratch. Among open models, GLM 5.2 comes closest to the frontier, placing third at innovating. Notably, the AI-Scientists beat the paper’s reproduced method in 84% of improve and 74% of innovate attempts (§F.1).

The leaderboards show which models score highest in FNI score, but not what kind of ability it reflects. We first compare the two modes directly. If improving an existing method and inventing a method from scratch measured the same skill, models would keep similar ranks across the two leaderboards. Instead, the relationship is loose (Figure 13). Some models are much stronger when building on source code, while others rank higher when forced to design from scratch. We therefore treat improve and innovate as related but distinct research abilities.

Is performance just a scaling effect? Better results could come from scaling the attempt in two ways: using more external compute, or doing more model-side work through longer trajectories and more trial-and-error. We do not find either pattern. Compute hours and agent turns explain almost none of the variance in scores (R2≤0.02R^{2}\leq 0.02, Figure 14a; turns are our provider-agnostic proxy for model-side effort, since token counts may not be available). The leading models therefore do not win by simply spending more; they make better use of the same setting.

Then what drives it? The quality of the research itself. An LLM judge reads every attempt, blind to its score, and rates it on five properties: creativity (was the idea genuinely new, and did it pay off), engineering (was the implementation substantial, building on the existing code), rigor (was the reported gain real and honestly measured), significance (how far it moved the metric), and depth (how thoroughly the problem was explored). These ratings track the models’ actual scores almost exactly (ρ=0.89\rho=0.89, Figure 14b): the models that win are the ones doing better research, not the ones trying hardest.

Research is contingent. Research is inherently random. A strong attempt does not always produce a high score: a creative idea can be implemented well and still fail empirically, and a great idea might not suit the current setting, while a simpler idea may happen to work. Aggregating across many environments lets us measure progress without pretending that research has no outcome variance.

4.2 Dataset

We preserve every scientist’s research in full, so we collect a set of research traces, released per environment, model, and run mode. We record the scientist’s research idea and their revisions, the method and the full turn-by-turn trajectory, and the per-experiment logs and scores (Table 4). We store each attempt as a version-controlled repository, so each preserves the complete development history rather than the final state alone.

In total, the corpus records roughly 6,400 hours of research being done (§H.1). With multiple scientists’ attempts, one environment accumulates multiple independent solutions to a fixed problem, each labeled with its measured improvement over the reproduced source result.

4.3 Gym

Finally, we raise a scientist of our own. We train Qwen3-8B (Qwen Team, 2025), a scientist small enough that whatever it learns must come from the world, with Tinker (Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), in two stages:

  • •

    Supervised fine-tuning. 1,000 examples drawn from the trajectories, each pairing a task specification with an attempt’s reasoning and final idea, cleaned so that no fabricated result survives. (details in §H)

  • •

    GRPO. We do off-policy group relative policy optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) on 1,500 already-scored ideas, rewarded by measured outcomes. Advantages are relative to the other ideas for the same task, and updates are clipped to a trust region around the SFT policy. The scientist trains only with execution.

A scientist this small cannot yet carry the whole loop: implementing and debugging a method over a long horizon is frontier work in itself. We therefore separate ideation from implementation (Si et al., 2026). The trained scientist proposes the idea, and a single fixed frontier implementer (GPT 5.6 Sol) executes every idea under identical conditions on ten held-out papers (§H.4), so only the idea’s origin varies. We prompt the implementer to follow exactly the ideator’s idea.

The gain is monotone. The median implemented idea scores 41 FNI from the base scientist, 84 after SFT, and 106 after GRPO (Figure 15); the mean rises from 51 to 90. Ideas from the trained scientist, faithfully implemented, reach the anchor of the frontier cohort. What it demonstrates is the mechanism: the world supplied the data, the reward, and the held-out exam, and a scientist raised on its trajectories proposes measurably better research. The training loop works end to end.

§ 5 Background

Autonomous scientific discovery and AI-Scientists.

Automating discovery is a long-standing goal. Early systems recovered natural laws and governing equations directly from data (Schmidt and Lipson, 2009; Cranmer et al., 2020; Udrescu and Tegmark, 2020), and robot scientists closed the loop from hypothesis to physical experiment (King et al., 2004; King et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2015). Within machine learning, automated search took over bounded parts of the pipeline: model and hyperparameter selection (Thornton et al., 2013; Feurer et al., 2015), neural architecture design (Zoph and Le, 2017; Real et al., 2019), and even the discovery of faster fundamental algorithms (Fawzi et al., 2022; Mankowitz et al., 2023). Program search guided by language models extended this to open mathematical and algorithmic problems (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). Language models then widened the scope toward the full workflow: tool-augmented systems run their own chemical experiments (Boiko et al., 2023; Bran et al., 2024), and agentic pipelines generate ideas, write code, and draft papers end to end (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025). A newer wave organizes many agents into collaborative or self-directed discovery loops (Schmidgall et al., 2025; Schmidgall and Moor, 2025; Ghareeb et al., 2026), and general-purpose AI-Scientists now attempt discovery across whole fields (Gottweis et al., 2025; Mitchener et al., 2025). This line builds better scientists; is complementary, turning finished papers into environments where such scientists can be handed the same problem and scored on it.

Measuring AI-Scientists.

Evaluating agents in executable settings began with general benchmarks for tool use and repository-level code editing (Jimenez et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Mialon et al., 2024), then moved to machine-learning experimentation and engineering (Huang et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025; Nathani et al., 2025). A parallel line probes scientific reasoning and data-driven discovery (Jansen et al., 2024; Majumder et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b), extending to hypothesis formation and frontier domain research (Liu et al., 2025; Miao et al., 2026). A closely related group scores whether an agent can reproduce a paper’s results from its description (Siegel et al., 2024; Starace et al., 2025), reimplement its method and code (Xiang et al., 2025; Hua et al., 2025), or take on research framed as an open-ended challenge (Zhang et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025a). These suites are almost always fixed and hand-curated, and critiques of agent evaluation warn that they can confound cost, leak through weak holdouts, and reward shortcuts (Kapoor et al., 2024). Concurrent work also turns real papers into research tasks but curates them by hand, which does not scale (Garikaparthi et al., 2026). instead treats construction itself as the object: it selects papers at scale and refactors each into a scored, reproduce-then-improve environment, so a method is judged by its gain over a faithfully reproduced result rather than its distance from a reported number.

§ 6 Conclusion

Every published paper with code is a finished piece of research: a problem, a method, and a measured result. turns that record back into a place where research happens: 1,000 papers become runnable, scored environments, and the collection grows with the literature rather than with annotation effort. The same environments measure today’s AI-Scientists and train the next ones; each is a scaled-down paper and each score one contingent trajectory, but the loop they are built for, a scientist that proposes, executes, and updates inside the world, is just beginning. As the models and the literature both move, the world keeps pace, and the problems it poses stay as open as the research it was built from.

Appendix A System Design

relies on agents that repeatedly alternate between reasoning and computation. This agent stack is the substrate that makes this loop practical at scale. It separates four concerns that are otherwise entangled: running compute jobs, bounding each experiment’s resource use, coordinating many papers, and normalizing different agent interfaces. We separate the system into four parts: Hive provides the compute pool; Nexus makes compute accountable to a particular attempt; Swarm coordinates many runs; and Worker presents each agent scaffold through the same interaction contract. Figure 16 summarizes these layers.

A.1 Hive: Interactive Compute Pool

Agent-driven reproduction needs a compute layer designed for interactive iteration. An agent may run a small debugging command, inspect the result, edit the code, and then launch a longer training or evaluation job. If every such step pays the full overhead of acquiring resources and preparing execution, the research loop becomes dominated by infrastructure latency rather than by scientific reasoning. Hive keeps compute capacity available, monitored, and controlled, so these iterations remain close to an interactive workflow.

Hive exposes compute as an experimental action: given a requested experiment, declared resources, and a workspace, it reports what happened. The result is not only a terminal success or failure label. It includes the execution evidence the agent needs to decide what to do next: logs, completion status, timing, and partial output when a job is still running. This matters because reproduction agents rarely need a single monolithic training run; they work through a trial and error sequence of tests, attempts, fixes, ablations, and evaluations. Figure 17 shows the execution path inside Hive.

Input.

Hive’s input is a job request. In our interface, the concrete entry point is a terminal command: hive submit, whose parameters specify what should run. --workdir anchors the run to the code and files it should see, --gpus and --cpus declare the requested capacity, --resource targets a named pool such as test, CPU, or GPU capacity, and --timeout-sec bounds jobs that hang or run past their intended scale. Optional fields such as retry count and log directory make the request easier to recover and inspect. These fields are useful because they turn an open shell command into a schedulable execution unit: Hive can decide where it can run, how much capacity it needs, when it should stop, and where its evidence should be recorded.

Output.

Hive returns a job identifier and maintains a job record, not an experiment-specific result file. The record directory contains meta.json, stdout.log, and stderr.log: metadata for status, timing, resource use, and return code, plus streamed logs for diagnosis. Any checkpoints, metrics, or plots created by the command remain in the working directory; Hive records how the execution went.

Elasticity.

A job asks for a category of resource (test, CPU, or GPU) and Hive places it on whatever node is free, without the agent naming a specific machine. The pool can grow or shrink as capacity becomes available, so the first worker to come online is useful immediately, and the same request format serves every experiment.

Node Types.

Hive exposes three node types through the same job interface. CPU nodes support CPU-only experiments, setup, preprocessing, and other jobs that do not require accelerators. GPU nodes run accelerator-heavy experiments such as training and large-scale evaluation. Test nodes are for quick code validation and small-scale testing, with jobs capped at one hour so agents do not tie up long-running allocations.

Reliability.

Long-running jobs are not perfectly reliable: a job can stall or be killed before it finishes, and its partial output is often still useful. Hive therefore treats an interruption as a reportable outcome rather than a silent failure: it writes the job’s last state and logs into the job record, then requeues it on another valid machine, where the command restarts from the beginning; the interrupted attempt is recorded for inspection like any completed one, and its incomplete work is not charged against the budget.

Implementation.

We use Ray (Moritz et al., 2018) to implement Hive. Ray starts each job on a free machine and runs it; everything else the compute pool needs for agent-driven reproduction is built on top. A resource manager tracks CPU, GPU, and test capacity; a dispatcher turns agent requests into queued jobs; an agent-facing client/API submits jobs and streams progress back; and a persistent job store records logs, status, and final outputs outside the Ray runtime. These pieces are what make the compute pool usable as research infrastructure, not just a distributed execution engine.

A.2 Nexus: Experiment Boundary

Nexus is the experiment boundary that manages the resources agents use. It is a bridge between agents and compute. An autonomous agent should not be trusted to enforce its own compute budget simply because the prompt tells it to be careful. Nexus makes the budget a property of the system. Each reproduction attempt receives a bounded project: jobs must fit within its resource limits, its concurrent usage cap, and its remaining GPU-hour budget before they are allowed to run. Compute is no longer something the agent can spend freely; every job is counted against the project’s budget. The operations view in Figure 18 shows these exchanges: agents submit or review jobs through Nexus, and Nexus communicates between infrastructures and agents.

Quota Semantics.

Nexus enforces several constraints that matter for reproducibility: how much compute a paper can spend in total, how much it can hold at once, which kinds of resources it may use, and how long any single job may run before it times out. At the job level, these limits cover CPU, GPU, memory, and time requests. These constraints are checked outside the agent. The project-level example in Figure 19 makes the gate concrete: a request can be rejected because it exceeds the remaining budget or concurrency capacity, or requests a resource pool outside the given policy.

Fairness.

This accounting matters for both fairness and interpretability. Without it, one agent can consume resources in ways that alter the conditions for others, and the resulting comparison would conflate scientific difficulty with uncontrolled resource use. With Nexus, the amount of compute available for a single reproduction is explicit and enforceable. The agent can still decide how to reasonably spend its budget, but it cannot silently exceed the given total.

Periodic Review.

Nexus makes long jobs interruptible without requiring the agent to keep an active turn open for the whole execution. At each configured review interval, Nexus snapshots the latest logs, records them in the workspace, and wakes the responsible agent to inspect them. The agent can then continue the run, cancel it, or change strategy before spending the remaining budget. Interval review pays off because many broken reproductions are visible well before natural termination: imports fail after setup, data paths are wrong, losses diverge, or an evaluator writes clearly invalid output. A run that would otherwise consume hours can stop after the first snapshot that shows it is going nowhere. If the agent does not respond within the review window, Nexus continues the job rather than leaving compute blocked by a missing response.

Separation.

This layer is intentionally separate from Hive, and can accept any compute infrastructure. Nexus is optimized for accountability. Keeping them separate prevents the compute pool from accumulating task-specific policy and prevents Swarm from having to reason about low-level execution state.

A.3 Swarm: Builder Coordination

Swarm has two jobs. The first is per paper: it drives one reproduction across many agent turns and several roles, keeping the attempt coherent as builders hand off, retry, and audit each other’s work. The second is across papers: it runs many of these attempts at the same time, each as its own trajectory, without their states blurring together. Both are hard because the work is open-ended. A reproduction can produce useful code without supporting the paper’s central claim, support the claim but leave no reusable environment, or produce scores that look plausible until a later audit checks them. If these judgments live only in chat transcripts, the result is a collection of anecdotes. Swarm therefore turns each paper attempt into an auditable trajectory: the assigned agent, budget, workspace state, results, milestone, and next role are explicit at every step. Figure 20 shows the end-to-end path: a pool of paper workspaces, each driven through an ordered role workflow under a milestone gate, ending in an artifact that is either accepted or set aside.

Pipeline.

Swarm turns a paper into a finished environment. Its builders reproduce the paper’s main claim, design the reproduction into a usable task, organize its files, and verify the result. Swarm does not run this in one long session. A builder works in short turns, and ends each turn with an action, usually submitting a compute job or signaling that it is done. Swarm tracks that action and the paper’s state, and whenever something changes it wakes the builder with a prompt written for that exact situation: for example, when a compute job finishes, a prompt that carries the results and asks what to do next; when a build fails, a prompt with the build log and a request to fix it; when one stage is complete, a prompt that briefs the agent for the next. The agent is therefore only ever asked to decide the one thing that just came up. Swarm runs this loop over a pool of many workers, so it advances a large number of papers at the same time.

Coordination.

Swarm answers the question that remains after a single agent turn ends: who should act next, and what do they inherit from the builder before them? Its unit of state is the paper, not the agent session: Swarm tracks where each paper sits in its workflow and the milestone it has reached, so a new builder resumes from the right point and can build on a partial result left by the previous one. This is what lets a single paper pass through several builders, even different models, and still read as one coherent attempt; without it, the final artifact would mix the paper’s difficulty with hidden differences in how the agent happened to be run.

Wake Events.

Swarm wakes a builder only when new information changes what it should decide: a fresh paper or a new role to begin, a running job it may continue or cancel, a finished job, a failed build, an exhausted budget, a validation or milestone-gate failure, or a role transition. The agent returns a structured action, and Swarm records both the action and what prompted it. Table 5 summarizes what is shown.

Completion Checks.

When a builder declares a pass finished, Swarm separates local correctness from progress. The local check confirms the action is parseable and the milestone label is canonical, then runs the workspace validator, which verifies that the score files exist, the evaluator is separated from the method, and the workspace rebuilds from a clean clone (§C.4). Failures become repair prompts, capped at three validation attempts. The progress check asks whether the claimed milestone clears the bar for the current stage; a run that falls short reverts to an earlier pass or stops (§A.3.3).

Worker Pool.

Swarm runs many paper workspaces through the same loop at once. It assigns idle Workers to saved workflow states, resumes the correct role after each turn, and sends experiment declarations to Nexus under that paper’s budget. The builder chooses the scientific next step; Swarm handles scheduling, accounting, and routing the returned evidence back to the right workspace.

A.3.1 Milestones

Progress Ladder.

Swarm measures progress with a canonical milestone ladder, not with a binary success flag. The main target in the standard workflow is core_claim: a minimum experiment must run the paper’s method and support the central claim. method_runs records weaker progress when the method executes but the claim is not yet supported; core_claim_plus, secondary_claims, majority, near_complete, and full record broader coverage; and not_possible records a case that should not be converted into an environment. These labels let Swarm preserve partial progress without recording it as success. The canonical labels are listed in Table 6. The agents self-report this.

Gating.

Milestones also determine whether the workflow should continue. If a builder declares completion below core_claim, Swarm gives one or more turns asking for additional evidence. If a required pass still falls short, Swarm can stop the trajectory or revert to an earlier pass. This keeps failed attempts inspectable without letting weak evidence advance.
