A.3.2 Builder Roles

Role Design.

Swarm does not give every agent the same job. It separates reproduction, environment design, packaging, and verification so that later agents can inspect and improve the artifacts left by earlier agents; we refer to these roles collectively as builders , the agents that construct an environment from a paper. Reproducers build and test the paper method; design agents convert a successful reproduction into a scored environment; the packager makes the workspace reusable; and verifiers audit whether the final milestone is supported by evidence. This role split keeps the workflow from depending on a single long agent session while still preserving one shared workspace. Table 7 summarizes the role responsibilities and the gate to satisfy.

Milestone Selection.

Each builder also chooses the milestone that best describes the current workspace after it is done. The choice is a self-evaluation against the canonical ladder in Table 6: the agent claims the milestone supported by runnable code, logs, scores, and notes, rather than simply reporting when the assigned role finishes. The label is a claim, not a verified fact, so it is never taken as final on its own: each later role and iteration inherits the same workspace and re-audits the previous agent’s claim, and the verifier lowers any milestone the workspace’s logs, scores, and code do not support. The bar for core_claim in particular is that the supporting run executes the paper’s own method on the paper’s task, possibly at reduced scale, and reproduces the direction of its central result, not merely that the code runs without error.

A.3.3 Workflow

Pass Sequence.

The standard workflow is an ordered list of stage rows (Figure 21). Each row specifies the model profile, role, GPU-hour budget, milestone cap, minimum milestone, and optional revert target for that pass. When a pass finishes, Swarm compares the claimed milestone with the row’s minimum requirement. Meeting the gate advances to the next row; falling below it triggers the configured revert target, or otherwise stops the trajectory as unsuccessful. Because the budget is attached to the row, routine checks stay small, experiment-heavy rows receive more room, and every paper is judged under the same stage-level limits.

Repeated Passes.

A workflow can include repeated rows for the same role. This is deliberate: a single builder round may leave partial progress, fragile evidence, or an unresolved design choice that should be inspected before the workflow advances. Repeated rows let the next agent continue from the saved workspace, try a different strategy, or audit the previous claim without treating the role as complete.

Multi-Agent Handoffs.

The handoff structure also makes the workflow a multi-agent process rather than a single long session. A later builder inherits the workspace, evidence, and gate left by the previous agent, so it can inspect earlier choices before extending them. This gives the system diversity in search strategy and reduces the chance that one mistaken assumption carries through the entire artifact. It also saves cost by placing lower-cost model profiles on routine continuation and reserving stronger profiles for difficult passes. Since the handoff includes the current milestone claim, each agent can revise the milestone selected by previous agents.

A.4 Worker: Agent Interface

We design Worker as one interface through which every agent scaffold CLI connects to the system. Scaffolds vary in how they are launched, resumed, and billed; Worker absorbs that variation so a model is judged on the research it produces, not on the scaffold that drives it. Figure 22 shows this path: heterogeneous scaffolds enter through one uniform turn interface, run inside a constrained container, and end each turn by writing an action.yaml that wakes the system for the next turn.

Turns and actions.

A session is a sequence of turns. The first turn sets the agent up in its workspace; every later turn is short, sent only when something changes, such as a finished job or a failed build. The agent ends a turn by writing one file, action.yaml, that states its decision, shown in Figure 23.

The agent makes its request in this fixed format. The system then processes it to decide the next step. action says whether to submit a job or declare the paper done; gpus and test set its size and route it to the full or the short test pool; milestone records the agent’s own assessment against the fixed milestone ladder. Because the agent never launches a job itself, the system can check every request, count it against the budget, and schedule it before it runs; a malformed one is handed back to rewrite, while the reasoning behind it survives in the turn record. The loop also removes any need to finish in a single session: the agent is re-engaged as jobs complete and builds fail, and progress accumulates between turns.

Containment.

We run the agent inside an Apptainer container (Kurtzer et al., 2017) whose home is the paper workspace. It sees only a base image and that workspace: the container hides the cluster’s home and temporary directories and drops all administrator bind mounts, so the shared filesystems are out of reach. Inside, it edits code freely, and the GPU jobs it later submits reuse the same layout, so no host path is ever exposed. Three limits keep one agent from starving its neighbors: a memory cap to bound total RAM, a low scheduler priority to make co-located agents yield CPU, and thread caps on the numeric libraries.

Dependencies.

Installing packages is separated from running jobs. The agent does not install during a job; it declares what it needs in two workspace files: environment/container.def for the base image and OS packages, and environment/setup.sh for Python packages. The system builds these once and keeps the result in a persistent overlay on top of the base image, so the packages are available to every later job without reinstalling or rebuilding the container. Editing either file triggers a rebuild before the next job runs.

Boundary and robustness.

We place a few things outside the agent’s reach by construction: the bookkeeping files and the recorded trajectory are hidden, the validator is read-only, and git push is disabled so the system decides when work is published. Turns are stripped of credential patterns before they are written, since the per-paper repositories may be made public. And because a paper can span thousands of unattended turns, Worker recovers on its own: it retries transient errors such as rate limits, switches to another model profile on terminal ones such as an exhausted usage cap, and kills a stalled turn along with its whole process tree.

A.5 How the Components Connect

Forward path.

The four components pass work to each other through recorded state, not inside one long agent session. Worker presents the paper and workspace to the agent and reads its action from action.yaml. Swarm owns the paper’s trajectory: it tracks the milestone, advances through the workflow of roles, prepares the workspace, and turns a submit action into a job request for Nexus. Nexus checks the project’s budget, its concurrency cap, and the requested resource pool, then forwards the job to Hive, which runs it.

Return path.

Results travel back through the same components. Hive reports the job’s state, return code, and resource usage; Nexus matches the finished job to its run record, writes the logs and outputs into the workspace, releases the GPUs it was holding, and charges the run against the project’s budget. Swarm reads the event, updates the paper’s state, and wakes the Worker for the next turn. Because everything lands as files the agent can open, not as hidden service state, a later turn or a different model can look back at what each job did and how it ended.

Why split it this way.

The split gives each component a single, narrow responsibility, and that is what keeps the system auditable. Worker can think and edit but cannot give itself compute; Swarm can coordinate papers but does not run jobs; Nexus enforces resource limits without judging scientific progress; Hive runs jobs without knowing which claim they support. Because the boundaries between them are clean, the four parts are meant to work independently, and any one of them can be swapped for a different implementation, a new scaffold, scheduler, or compute backend, without touching the others. The final artifact is tied to both sides: the agent trajectory that produced it, and the run records that make that trajectory checkable.

Appendix B Builder Design

runs entirely on autonomous agents: every environment is produced by builders that reproduce a paper and shape the result into a task, with no human in the loop. This section describes how those builders work and the principles that decide whether the environment they leave behind is a good one. Figure 24 gives the overview: from a paper and an empty workspace, builders produce a reusable environment across problem definition, method reproduction, and evaluation.

B.1 What the Builders Do

The task.

§A described the system that runs the builders; this section is about the research task it is built for. Given a single published paper, the agents must reproduce the paper’s central result and leave behind a reusable environment, an executable setup in which a later scientist can attempt to improve on that result. This is the foundation everything else rests on, since an environment whose method was never really implemented would have nothing to measure. The rest of this subsection traces what the agents actually do, from the paper to the finished environment and how each turn is driven; the design choices behind that environment follow in §B.2.

From paper to environment.

A builder’s input is the paper itself, in both Markdown and PDF with its figures, together with a fresh, empty workspace. The reproducer starts from this and proceeds in order. It first reads the paper and writes a short briefing, separating the problem and the evaluation protocol from the paper’s method, and transcribes the paper’s reported numbers into a reference scoring file. It then prepares the environment: downloading the data and any model weights in advance, writing an evaluator that scores outputs without depending on the method, and checking that the scoring file is well formed. With that in place it implements the method and reproduces incrementally, submitting compute jobs to get one experiment that supports the core claim running before expanding to further settings, and recording its measured numbers alongside the paper’s. Reproduction usually spans several agents in turn: each later one inherits the saved workspace, audits what the previous agent built, and pushes it further.

Finishing the environment.

A working reproduction is not yet a usable environment. Once the method runs and supports the claim, a designer adds the visible and hidden evaluation slices and the scripts that produce their scores; a packager makes the workspace rebuild from a clean clone, with every dataset and model fetched by a self-contained download script; and a verifier audits the whole artifact before it is accepted. How these roles are sequenced, what budget each receives, and how progress is graded are handled by the system (§A.3); what each role leaves in the workspace is detailed in §C.

How a builder is prompted.

The builder works in turns, ending each by requesting a compute job or declaring the work done, and runs fully autonomously with no human in the loop (§A.4). Because a paper can span thousands of unattended turns, it is not given one fixed instruction. Where §A.3 describes when an agent is woken and what state it is shown, here the point is what it is then asked to do: the first turn carries the full role briefing, and every later turn is a short prompt written for the condition that woke it. Table 8 lists the main conditions and the instruction each prompt carries.

B.2 Design Choices

A good environment does not come from reproducing a paper alone; it also has to be designed so that a later method can be tested fairly on it, all under a limited compute budget. We follow seven design choices toward this, each stated first and then explained.

The goal is to make the paper’s method run, not to match a table entry. Exact-number reproduction rewards the wrong behavior: a builder could tune toward the published values, or copy them outright, without implementing the method. Instead, the environment should contain the paper’s actual computation and produce reasonable support for the claimed effect. A simple check is whether a reader of the code can recognize the algorithm from the paper.

Most papers cannot be reproduced at full scale under a fixed budget. The builder may therefore reduce the model size, dataset size, or number of training steps, which also keeps reproductions friendlier to the broader community using the artifact. What it may not do is change the procedure. If the paper trains from scratch, the environment trains from scratch. If the paper uses a particular optimization setup, the environment keeps that setup. Resources can shrink; the experiment cannot become a different experiment.

Scaling down also has a limit. A task made too small becomes trivial, and a trivial task cannot distinguish the paper’s method from a weak baseline. When a builder uses a smaller or synthetic dataset, it must check that a basic baseline does not already solve the problem. If the reproduced method is no better than random guessing, majority class, or another weak baseline within noise, the reproduction has failed. The environment needs a real gap so that future agents have something meaningful to improve.

This boundary keeps the problem definition independent of the solution that produced it. The problem, its data, and its evaluator can be stated and run without the paper’s method, so the environment poses the problem on its own terms rather than only as a continuation of one particular implementation; the file boundary is described in §C.2. The separation also protects the score. If the evaluator secretly depended on the reproduced method, then changing the method might not change what is measured, and the environment would look functional while no longer testing the intended problem.

The separation must hold at runtime, not only in the file layout. The evaluator must read the outputs a method produced, never call the method’s code: if deleting method/ would change the evaluation scores, the boundary is broken. Likewise, the data loaders belong to the problem, not the solution, and must not import from method/. The evaluate scripts must also discover methods dynamically, enumerating whatever methods exist on disk rather than hardcoding a name, so that the evaluator works for a future method without editing. How the environment is then presented to a future agent is a matter for evaluation (§E.1).

The finished environment includes an evaluation suite that a future scientist can see and optimize against. If that suite is only one metric on one dataset, the easiest path may be to game that number rather than improve the underlying idea. To reduce this risk, the designer builds two slices: a visible slice for development and a hidden slice that is run only after done. A large gap between the two suggests overfitting or shortcuts.

The split can be drawn in different ways, depending on the paper: held-out samples, held-out subgroups, harder inputs, or several related metrics that measure the same claim from different angles. Using multiple metrics from different angles is stronger than a single held-out number, because a single metric can be gamed while triangulation from several directions catches shortcuts that any one metric would miss.

The hidden slice must be calibrated against the visible one in difficulty: both should probe the method at roughly equal rigor, using matched data scales, evaluation protocols, and sample counts. An honest method should score similarly on both; if the hidden slice is simply harder, then every method will look worse there and the gap will be meaningless. The two slices should also be independent, so reading or importing the visible evaluator does not reveal the hidden one. And the test slice should be lightweight: it re-scores existing artifacts or slices them differently, rather than retraining or re-running expensive inference.

An environment should allow future methods to improve on the paper. For that reason, the score must not measure distance from the paper’s published number. Such a metric would make the paper’s own method the target and turn the environment into a reproduction-fidelity test. The paper’s reported numbers should be recorded as context, but future methods should be scored on the underlying quantity: accuracy, loss, robustness, sample efficiency, parameter count, or whatever the claim is actually about.

This principle is enforced in the scoring schema: metric names that encode closeness to the paper, such as deviation, vs_paper, or agreement_with, are blocked by the validator, so the score must name the underlying scientific quantity.

The environment must also define what stays fixed. A future scientist should not win by using more compute, a larger model, more data, or a different training paradigm unless that is the allowed direction of improvement. For papers that claim a benefit without a cost, the evaluator should measure both sides: the benefit that should improve and the constraint that should not break. The scoring contract expresses this through metric coefficients: a positive coefficient marks a benefit to maximize, a negative one marks a constraint that must not degrade, and the experiment weights reflect how central each result is to the paper’s claim.

Hardware varies from run to run, so a latency or wall-clock measurement can swing severalfold with no change to the method, and an environment that scored it would reward landing on a faster GPU rather than finding a better idea. Scores therefore use quantities that are stable across machines: parameter count, FLOPs, training steps, examples processed, or final task performance. When the paper’s own claim is about speed or efficiency, the environment keeps the claim but measures it through a machine-independent proxy rather than the clock.

A one-number reproduction is too thin a target. A future scientist may match it and still have little room to learn from or improve. Once the core claim runs, the environment should expand along the axes the paper itself studies: datasets, input difficulty, model scale, ablations, data regimes, or other relevant settings. A small matrix over two meaningful axes is usually more useful than repeated runs of the same setting.

This matrix does not need to be large. It needs to expose the structure of the claim. Combined with the non-triviality check above, it turns the environment from a single point estimate into one with headroom: weak baselines leave a gap, the reproduced method occupies a recognizable starting point, and future methods have several genuine ways to improve.

An environment that only works on the machine that built it is not reusable. The download script must fetch every dataset, model weight, and external resource from a public source using executable commands, not comments or placeholder URLs. It must be idempotent and must not reference local shared paths that exist only on the original cluster. The container definition and setup script must declare every system and Python dependency so that the software rebuilds without manual intervention. And every local import in the evaluation, method, and baseline code must resolve to a file tracked by git, so that a fresh clone contains everything the experiments need to run.

The validator enforces this: it scans committed code for references to machine-local shared directories and checks that every import target is a tracked file. Together with the reproducible-execution scripts (§C.3), this makes the environment a portable artifact rather than a snapshot of one session’s state.

Appendix C Agent Workspace

The workspace is the single directory the builders work in and the artifact they leave behind. Its layout is what makes the result a reusable environment rather than the residue of one run. We describe its structure (§C.1), its problem statement and scoring (§C.2), its execution (§C.3), and its records and checks (§C.4).

C.1 Structure

Overview.

Each paper is reproduced inside a single working directory, and that directory is also the artifact the builders leave behind. During the run it holds the code, data, experiments, and notes; once the run ends, it is designed to stand on its own, so that another party can clone it, rebuild the environment, rerun the method, and obtain the same scores without access to the original session. This is what distinguishes a reusable research environment from the residue of a single successful run, in which the method is entangled with the evaluator, the data exists only in a local cache, and the scores carry no well-defined meaning. The layout shown in Figure 25 is designed to prevent these failures.

File Roles.

The layout is a deliberate design choice rather than a storage convention: each directory has a single responsibility. The briefing defines what a future scientist may know; method/ and baseline/ hold what the reproducer built; data/ and eval/ define the problem interface that any method must satisfy; scoring/ defines how a method is judged; and scripts/ and environment/ determine whether the workspace runs outside the original session. Table 9 summarizes the groups.

C.2 Problem and Scoring

Problem and Solution Boundary.

The workspace deliberately separates the problem from the solution so that the problem is method-agnostic: it states what must be achieved and how it is measured, without revealing the paper’s approach. This is what allows the workspace to serve as a fair task for any future method rather than a recreation of one particular solution. The boundary appears in two places. In the briefing, problem.md gives the research question and success criteria and evaluation.md the metrics and protocol, neither naming the method; only method.md describes the paper’s approach, and overview.md summarizes the finished workspace. In the code, method/ contains the reproduced algorithm, while eval/ and data/ are written to work for any method, so a score never depends on the specific implementation. Because the problem stands on its own, an innovate scientist can attempt it from the briefing and evaluator alone, whereas an improve scientist additionally receives method/ as a starting point (§E).

Scoring Contract.

Scoring is held in two files. scoring/reference.json records the paper’s reported numbers for each baseline and proposed method, along with the scoring rules: a weight per experiment, set by the agents to reflect how central that result is to the paper’s core claim (weights sum to one), the direction of each metric, and a label marking each method as a baseline or a proposed method. scoring/scores.json holds the numbers the reproduction actually produced. A later method is scored by its improvement over those reproduced numbers, in each metric’s direction and combined by the weights, so the score measures progress over the reproduction rather than closeness to the paper. Figure 26 shows the two files side by side.

Targets and Constraints.

The JSON files fix the numbers, but a scientist also requires the intent behind them. Four short markdown files provide it: TARGETS.md states what to optimize, CONSTRAINTS.md states what must remain fixed, DIRECTION.md states which kinds of change are permitted, and EXPERIMENTS.md describes each scored experiment without disclosing the method. Together they exclude trivial gains, such as substituting a larger model, adding unrelated data, or altering the problem itself, while preserving room for a genuine methodological improvement. For example, an agent may improve performance on a Mamba architecture optimization problem by replacing the architecture with a Transformer. While this could yield better results, such a change provides no scientific value, as it sidesteps the original problem rather than advancing our understanding of how to improve Mamba models themselves. When a paper makes a trade-off claim, both sides must be scored: the benefit and the constraint it must not violate. Otherwise the easiest route to a high score is to break the very condition the paper was designed to satisfy.

C.3 Execution

Reproducible Execution.

The workspace must be able to rebuild from source, not only on the machine where it was created. scripts/download.sh fetches external data, weights, and other public resources; it must be idempotent and must not reference local shared paths. environment/container.def captures the system dependencies and environment/setup.sh the packages. scripts/method.sh then runs the reproduced method, scripts/baseline.sh runs the comparisons, scripts/evaluate.sh scores the outputs through eval/, and scripts/reproduce.sh runs the full pipeline end to end. The workspace is therefore an executable artifact rather than a static record of results: a fresh clone rebuilds the environment, reruns the method, and regenerates the score files.

Visible and Held-Out Slices.

A finished workspace also includes a train/test split for the scientist who reuses it. The visible slice, eval/train/, is what a future agent develops against; the held-out slice, eval/test/, lives in the environment’s pristine source copy and is materialized into a run only for the final score, so it is never present in the agent’s working tree during development. The paired scripts/evaluate_train.sh and scripts/evaluate_test.sh write scores_train.json and scores_test.json. The purpose of the split is not to make the paper harder to reproduce but to detect a future agent that has overfit the visible evaluator.

C.4 Records and Validation

Design Summary.

Each choice in the workspace exists to rule out a specific way it could fail to transfer to a new scientist. Figure 27 collects them: the design decision, the failure it prevents, and where it lives.

Reproduction Record.

When a run ends, the system writes a manifest.json into the workspace and compiles a README.md containing a per-iteration reproduction log, alongside the git history that checkpoints every turn. Together these tie the result to recorded state rather than to the conversation, allowing a later agent or reviewer to trace how it was reached. Table 10 groups the fields the manifest records.

Acceptance Checks.

A workspace is checked before it is accepted. validate.py runs automatically and enforces the scoring schema, blocks the obvious paper-agreement metric names, and checks the structural rules that keep the workspace independent of its own method and rebuildable from a fresh clone; Table 11 lists the checks in full. The markdown audit files then cover what code cannot decide: MILESTONES.md states the claimed milestone, PROGRESS.md and VERIFICATION.md record why it is justified and what was changed from the paper, and CHECKLIST.md confirms that the workspace is ready for both improve and innovate mode reuse. A workspace is accepted only when the automatic checks pass and the audit files are complete.

Version Control.

Every workspace is a git repository, and the system commits to it continuously, so the full trajectory can be replayed from the repository alone, without the session that produced it. Each agent edit is committed as it is made, and each job submission is committed together with the exact code it ran, so the state behind any result is pinned to a specific revision. When a job finishes, its logs are written back into the workspace and committed as tracked files, so what ran and what it produced live in the same history as the code. The builder cannot publish: git push is disabled, and the system decides when it is released (§A.4).

Evaluation reuses the same git-backed design with one branch per attempt. Each time a model is run on an environment, that attempt is isolated on its own branch, so attempts never interfere, and each one can be inspected, rescored, or rerun on its own from the committed state it started from.

Appendix D Selecting Papers

Not every paper can or should become a suitable environment. A useful task has to be both worth reproducing and feasible for an autonomous builder to attempt under a bounded budget. Before any reproduction begins, we therefore narrow a large pool of recent papers down to a smaller, category-balanced set through a staged pipeline: cheap model screens drop low-quality and off-type papers, a deeper analysis scores each remaining paper for quality and reproduction difficulty, and a final ranking and balancing step chooses the papers we attempt. The rest of this section walks through that pipeline and reports how many papers survive each stage.

Candidate Pool.

We assemble the candidate pool before any builder is launched. Our selection snapshot is exported from a global arXiv index of 124,816 unique papers. The index is built from daily category listings between January 1, 2025 and March 1, 2026, and exported on March 28, 2026. We restrict the source categories to cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.AI, and cs.LG (Figure 29), then deduplicate by arXiv ID because the same paper can appear under more than one category. We also drop papers whose primary category is statistics (the stat.* group), which are dominated by theoretical work that offers little to execute or reproduce. This gives the candidate pool a temporal and topical boundary before any model is asked to judge feasibility. Figure 28 reports how many papers survive each screening stage from this pool onward.

Fast Screening.

Before any model reads a paper, we convert its PDF into Markdown with MinerU (Wang et al., 2024), which extracts the text, tables, and figures into a clean form that the screening and analysis models can read directly. The first two passes over this text are cheap, high-recall screens rather than final selection rules. Each pass sees only the opening 15,000 characters of the converted paper, which typically span the abstract and introduction, so that screening cost stays low across the full index. The first pass returns a quality score: MiniMax M2.7 (MiniMax, 2026) reads the excerpt and emits a short justification together with an integer rating from 0 to 100. A second pass assigns each paper one of five types: metric-method, benchmark/dataset, analysis/findings, theoretical, or survey/position. The quality screen is broad: 94.3% of scored papers are at least 50, 40.5% are at least 70, and only 12.0% reach 80 or higher. The type screen is more selective in the direction needs: 94,161 papers, or 75.9%, are labeled metric-method. Figure 30 reports the full quality-score and paper-type distributions. The quality screen is the gate into deep analysis: structured analysis runs only within the top quality band, papers scoring 75 or higher (33,393 papers, the top 26.9%), and 21,354 of them complete the analysis under the analysis budget. The fast type label guides this stage but does not filter it; the decisive type filter uses the structured analysis’s own classification and appears as the first drops in Figure 32.

Structured Analysis.

Papers carried forward from the fast screens go through a deeper analysis with MiniMax M2.7 (MiniMax, 2026), which classifies each paper and records a reproduction-oriented catalog entry. The first and most decisive field is the paper type. We keep only method papers, whose contribution is a method or technique evaluated with measurable results, and set aside the other four types: benchmark or dataset papers, where the contribution is the evaluation rather than a method; analysis or findings papers, which report observations rather than improvements; theoretical papers, whose contribution is a formal result; and survey or position papers, which carry no original experiments. Only method papers fit a reproduce-then-improve task, where an agent has to implement a method and then improve on a measured number.

The remaining fields describe each surviving paper in more detail: contribution novelty, taxonomy, compute and paid-resource requirements, benchmarks, datasets, baselines, concrete dependencies on other papers, code availability, reproduction difficulty, research quality, and problem novelty, with every scalar judgment given as an integer score from 0 to 10. Reproduction difficulty is split into coding, compute, time to run, and data or model difficulty, plus an overall score, because a paper should not be chosen on scientific appeal alone; a useful task also has to be feasible for an autonomous agent under a bounded budget. Figure 31 shows how these scores are distributed across the analyzed papers.

Filtering and Ranking.

The final selection balances importance against feasibility. Let qq be the 0-10 paper quality score, and let rr be the aggregate reproduction difficulty. When all four reproduction subscores are present, we compute

r=5​roverall+1.25​(rcode+rcompute+rspeed+rdata)10.r=\frac{5r_{\mathrm{overall}}+1.25(r_{\mathrm{code}}+r_{\mathrm{compute}}+r_{\mathrm{speed}}+r_{\mathrm{data}})}{10}.

It then ranks eligible papers by u=(q/10)​(1−r/10)u=\sqrt{(q/10)(1-r/10)}, so a paper must be both scientifically strong and reasonably reproducible to rank highly. Code availability is recorded but is not a hard requirement, which allows to include papers where agents must reconstruct missing pieces. The filtering counts in Figure 32 are sequential counts from the exported snapshot, each paper attributed to its first rejecting rule.

Category Balancing.

The feasible pool is still highly uneven across topics, so we do not simply take the top 1,000 utility scores. We first map fine-grained taxonomy labels into 18 canonical categories, then allocate final slots using temperature-smoothed category shares with temperature 1.21.2. The largest categories remain large, but smaller categories are not squeezed out entirely. Figure 33 shows the candidate pool and selected count for each canonical category. Figure 34 reads the resulting environments in their own words: what each asks to make better, and the work delivering it requires.

Appendix E Evaluation Protocol

Evaluation is the scoring harness that turns the reproduced environments into comparable scores across models. Where Swarm is built for open-ended builder coordination, Evaluation is deliberately flatter: it runs one controlled trial for each combination of paper, model, and mode. Each trial starts from a fresh workspace, receives a bounded compute budget through Nexus, drives one agent session through reason-run-feedback turns, and records the resulting train and held-out test scores. The harness splits this into auditable stages, from scaffolding through normalization (Table 12). The unit of comparison is therefore explicit: a model is judged by what its agent can build under the same problem statement, workspace boundary, scoring contract, and compute budget. We call this evaluated agent the scientist agent, to distinguish it from the builders that construct an environment (§A.3.2).

E.1 Evaluation Modes

Each environment can be run in two modes that ask different questions of a model. In improve mode, the scientist is given the reproduced method and the train-phase scores it already achieves, and must push those numbers higher without changing the evaluation protocol; the question is whether the model can advance an existing result. In innovate mode, the agent is given only the problem statement, the constraints and targets, the visible evaluator, and the data interface, with an empty method directory, and must build a method from first principles; the question is whether the model can solve the problem on its own.

The two modes are the problem-and-solution separation of §B.2 made operational: the same environment, presented once with the reproduced method and once without it. This separation is built into the workspace layout, not just the prompt. The reproduced method lives in its own method/ directory, while the problem statement, scoring targets, visible evaluator, and data interface sit outside it, and the evaluator and data never import from method/ (§C). Because the rest of the environment does not depend on the method, a single change switches modes: method/ is handed over intact for improve mode and emptied for innovate mode. They are kept separate in both the run matrix and the normalization, because a score earned by inventing a method from scratch is not the same experimental object as one earned by improving an existing method.

E.2 Running a Trial

Workspace Boundary.

Evaluation controls what the scientist can see and modify. The problem briefing, data, baseline artifacts, and visible training evaluator are read-only. The method directory, run scripts, scratch directory, and scoring directory are writable. Held-out test files, test scripts, reference scores, and the paper text are not present during the main phase. This boundary prevents agents from tuning against the hidden test split while still giving them enough information to conduct real research: they can read the task, implement a method, run the visible evaluator, inspect failures, and iterate. In improve mode, the starting method’s train score is copied into the briefing as a target to beat, but it is not used as an oracle during scoring.

Scientist Loop.

At the end of each turn, the scientist declares whether it wants to submit a compute job or finish. A submitted job runs the workspace’s compute entrypoint through Nexus, using the requested CPU or GPU resources and optionally the short test capacity for smoke tests. Evaluation does not implement its own execution loop; it consumes the job results that Nexus exposes and resumes the same agent session with them. Current runs use a 200-turn ceiling, and a trial that fails for a transient reason before producing any score file is retried up to three times. Once scoring files exist, the workspace is kept for review rather than overwritten.

Train and Test Scores.

The main phase produces scores_train.json using the visible evaluator. A host-side validator then checks the output against the source scoring shape: for every required proposed method, every numeric metric present in the reference reproduction must also be present in the agent’s score file. Metrics marked as baselines are ignored because they are not the scientist’s responsibility.

After train validation passes, the method the scientist built is frozen: its directory is mounted read-only before the held-out evaluator runs, so the test score reflects exactly the method that produced the train score and cannot be tuned against the hidden split. Evaluation then materializes the held-out evaluator from a pristine clone, so the scientist cannot influence what the test runs, and executes against the frozen method.

If the test job fails, the default recovery path keeps the method and the hidden evaluator read-only for five repair turns, so the scientist can repair missing packages or regenerate artifacts without modifying the frozen method or peeking at held-out data. If those turns do not succeed, a final three-turn path makes method/ writable again under a stricter honesty prompt, so a genuine interface mismatch can be repaired; even then the held-out evaluator and test data stay read-only and re-materialized from the pristine clone, so the method can be fixed but the hidden split still cannot be read nor the scorer altered, and these unlock turns are flagged in the trace. A run is complete only when both train and test score files validate.

E.3 Scoring

Evaluation reduces each model to one comparable number per paper, its FNI, then averages over the ten into a leaderboard. The raw measurements are heterogeneous at three levels. Within a paper, the result is split across experiments and their metrics, which sit on different scales, so one in the hundreds must not swamp one in hundredths, and carry different importance, so a metric central to the claim should count more than an incidental one. Across papers, the natural improvement ranges from a fraction of a percent to tens of points, yet every paper should contribute equal magnitude rather than let large-swing papers dominate. Across models, the comparison must stay fixed: a later model is scored against numbers frozen at publication rather than re-baselined, with the sign preserved and no value clamped. The scoring function below reconciles these levels, one cell at a time.

Definitions.

The scoring is built on the following objects, all fixed before any model is scored.

  • •

    Reference cohort ℳ={m1,…,mK}\mathcal{M}=\{m_{1},\dots,m_{K}\}: a fixed set of KK models, chosen once and frozen at publication. Each mkm_{k} is one model, and every model in ℳ\mathcal{M} is run on every paper.

  • •

    Cell cc: one metric of one method in one experiment. A single paper has many cells, spread across its experiments and the several metrics each one reports; baseline methods are excluded, leaving only the proposed methods.

  • •

    Source value scs_{c}: the value the paper’s own method reaches on cell cc once reproduced; it is the reference every model is measured against.

  • •

    Model value xm,cx_{m,c}: the value reached on cell cc by the method that model mm builds.

  • •

    Direction dc∈{+1,−1}d_{c}\in\{+1,-1\}: +1+1 when a higher value is better, −1-1 when lower is better.

  • •

    Prior weight pc=we⁡(c)​|κc|p_{c}=w_{e(c)}\,\lvert\kappa_{c}\rvert: how central the cell is to the paper’s claim, set by the builder when it writes the reference scoring file, not inferred from any model’s results. The agent records two numbers there: a weight wew_{e} for each experiment, normalized to sum to one across the paper, and a coefficient κc\kappa_{c} for each metric that sets the metrics within an experiment against one another. The prior weight is their product, taking the coefficient’s magnitude so that a metric’s direction (already captured by dcd_{c}) does not affect its weight.

The cohort is fixed because it calibrates every paper: adding a model to it would move every paper’s scale and baseline and invalidate all stored coefficients, so a later model is scored against the cohort, never added to it.

Cell Improvement.

The signed improvement of model mm on cell cc is

δm,c=dc​(xm,c−sc)={xm,c−sc,if higher is better,sc−xm,c,if lower is better,\delta_{m,c}=d_{c}(x_{m,c}-s_{c})=\begin{cases}x_{m,c}-s_{c},&\text{if higher is better},\\ s_{c}-x_{m,c},&\text{if lower is better},\end{cases}

positive for an improvement over the source and negative for a regression, on every metric. Every scale below is built from these improvements: how widely they spread across the cohort sets the unit for each cell, and the cohort’s typical paper score sets the baseline that makes papers comparable.

Cohort Scale.

For each paper, mode, and phase, the cohort fixes the scale that each cell is divided by. The first quantity is the per-cell spread,

σc=sdm∈ℳ⁡(δm,c)=1K−1​∑m∈ℳ(δm,c−δ¯c)2,δ¯c=1K​∑m∈ℳδm,c,\sigma_{c}=\operatorname{sd}_{m\in\mathcal{M}}(\delta_{m,c})=\sqrt{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\big(\delta_{m,c}-\bar{\delta}_{c}\big)^{2}},\qquad\bar{\delta}_{c}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\delta_{m,c},

the sample standard deviation of the cohort’s improvements on cell cc, where δ¯c\bar{\delta}_{c} is the cohort’s mean improvement on that cell. We use σc\sigma_{c} as the cell’s unit because it is expressed in the metric’s own scale: a metric reported in the hundreds gives a σc\sigma_{c} in the hundreds and one reported in hundredths gives a σc\sigma_{c} in hundredths, so dividing an improvement by σc\sigma_{c} removes the metric’s scale and lets cells be compared. Some cells have σc=0\sigma_{c}=0, where the cohort returns the same value and the cell carries no spread of its own; we want neither to drop these cells nor to divide by zero, so we also compute a fallback, the paper’s typical spread,

τ=medianj:σj>0σj,\tau=\operatorname*{median}_{j\,:\,\sigma_{j}>0}\ \sigma_{j},

the median of the nonzero per-cell spreads. A median, not a mean, keeps one unusually noisy cell from inflating this typical scale and shrinking every other cell. The per-cell normalizer then uses each cell’s own spread when it has one and τ\tau otherwise,

nc={σc,σc>0,τ,σc=0​ and ​τ>0,n_{c}=\begin{cases}\sigma_{c},&\sigma_{c}>0,\\ \tau,&\sigma_{c}=0\text{ and }\tau>0,\end{cases}

so a tied cell still contributes, scaled by the paper’s typical spread. If even τ=0\tau=0, no cell on the paper carries any spread, the paper has no usable scale, and it is excluded rather than scored with an arbitrary fallback.

Scale from the Cohort, not the Source.

For a cell the cohort does not tie on, the normalizer from the previous paragraph is simply the cohort spread, nc=σcn_{c}=\sigma_{c}. Dividing by this spread, rather than by the source value, is what places metrics of different scales on a common footing. The more obvious choice would divide each improvement by its source value, δm,c/|sc|\delta_{m,c}/|s_{c}|; but σc\sigma_{c} is computed from those same improvements, so dividing them by |sc||s_{c}| scales the cell and its spread alike, and the source value cancels:

δm,c/|sc|sdm⁡(δm,c/|sc|)=δm,c/|sc|σc/|sc|=δm,cσc,sc≠0.\frac{\delta_{m,c}/|s_{c}|}{\operatorname{sd}_{m}(\delta_{m,c}/|s_{c}|)}=\frac{\delta_{m,c}/|s_{c}|}{\sigma_{c}/|s_{c}|}=\frac{\delta_{m,c}}{\sigma_{c}},\qquad s_{c}\neq 0.

The cohort spread, not the source value, carries the scale. Writing the standardized cell score with the general normalizer,

zm,c=δm,cnc,z_{m,c}=\frac{\delta_{m,c}}{n_{c}},

and scs_{c} sets only the zero point of the improvement, not its scale. The score also stays well defined when scs_{c} is zero or near zero (for example, when a metric counts the number of bugs in a code snippet), where dividing by the source value would be undefined or blow a tiny gap into an enormous ratio.

Effective Weights.

The prior weight pcp_{c} records how important a metric is to the paper, but not how much it tells one model apart from another. A cell on which the whole cohort lands at nearly the same value carries little signal about which model is better, while a cell on which the cohort spreads out widely both separates models and is statistically reliable. We therefore scale each prior by the cell’s spread σc\sigma_{c} relative to the paper’s typical spread τ\tau, and renormalize so the weights sum to one:

w~c=pc​(β+σcσc+τ),wc=w~c∑jw~j.\tilde{w}_{c}=p_{c}\left(\beta+\frac{\sigma_{c}}{\sigma_{c}+\tau}\right),\qquad w_{c}=\frac{\tilde{w}_{c}}{\sum_{j}\tilde{w}_{j}}.

Here β\beta is a floor we set to 0.50.5. The weight wcw_{c} this produces is each cell’s share of the paper score, so scaling it by the cell’s spread makes the score lean on the cells that actually separate models and discount those that do not. When the cohort ties on a cell (σc=0\sigma_{c}=0), every model scores it the same, so the cell cannot tell a better model from a worse one; counting it at full weight would only dilute the score with a cell that carries no signal, so the factor drops to its floor β=0.5\beta=0.5, halving its influence without dropping it. When a cell spreads the cohort by the paper’s typical amount (σc=τ\sigma_{c}=\tau), it carries a representative amount of signal and the factor stays at 1.01.0, leaving its prior unchanged. When the cohort disagrees on a cell far more than usual (σc≫τ\sigma_{c}\gg\tau), the cell sharply separates models and is the most informative, so the factor rises toward 1.51.5 and the cell counts for up to half again its prior. The factor saturates smoothly toward β+1\beta+1 rather than being clipped at a hard cap.

This does a different job from the normalizer: ncn_{c} puts every cell on a common scale, while wcw_{c} sets how much each cell then counts. Together they keep any single cell, an extreme-scale metric or a tied, uninformative one, from deciding a paper’s score by itself. As a final backstop against a near-tied cell whose tiny spread inflates its coefficient, any cell whose contribution both outweighs all of a paper’s other cells combined and exceeds one full paper score in magnitude is pruned, uniformly for every model, so no saturated metric can swing a paper’s score on its own.

Paper Coefficients.

The cohort model’s score on a paper is the weighted sum of its standardized cell scores,

Rm=∑cwc​zm,c.R_{m}=\sum_{c}w_{c}\,z_{m,c}.

The size of RmR_{m} still varies across papers: a paper whose metrics swing widely gives every model a large RmR_{m}, and would dominate a leaderboard that averaged raw paper scores. To put papers on equal footing, we divide by the cohort’s typical paper-score magnitude on that paper,

b=1|ℳ|​∑m∈ℳ|Rm|,b=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}|R_{m}|,

the mean absolute RmR_{m} over the cohort. After dividing by bb, the cohort’s typical paper score has magnitude one on every paper, so each paper contributes equally to a model’s average instead of in proportion to how large its improvements happen to be. Weight, normalizer, and baseline then fold into a single stored coefficient per cell,

αc=wcnc​b,\alpha_{c}=\frac{w_{c}}{n_{c}b},

so a future model is scored by the frozen sum

S=∑cαc​δc.S=\sum_{c}\alpha_{c}\delta_{c}.

All spread estimates, weight adjustments, and paper baselines are absorbed into αc\alpha_{c} and never re-estimated.

Leaderboard.

Train and held-out test phases, and innovate and improve modes, keep separate coefficients because they measure different experimental objects. Within each published setting, the leaderboard reports the mean paper score over published papers. The scale comes from the reference cohort, and FNI is this score scaled by 100: a paper’s typical score across the cohort has magnitude 100, so a model that matches the cohort scores about 100, a model with about half again as much improvement scores near 150150, and a model at half the cohort’s gains scores near 5050; the score is positive when the model improves over the source reproduction and negative when it regresses. Because each paper’s spread across the cohort is about one, averaging over many published papers shrinks the noise in a model’s mean score, so models are separated by the average of many per-paper differences rather than by any single paper; we therefore read only sustained gaps as real and treat very close scores as ties. A paper is excluded from publication uniformly for every model, never per submission, when the cohort gives no usable scale (every cell tied, or a baseline that cancels to zero) or is too small to estimate spread (fewer than three cohort models present).

Appendix F Evaluation Analysis

The main text reads these environments as a leaderboard. Here we examine the evaluation behind it, asking three questions: how often a scientist actually improves on the reproduced method, whether a score reflects a real gain rather than a metric optimized during the run, and whether the number is largely a proxy for how much compute or interaction a run was given. In short: usually, yes, and no.

F.1 How Often Scientists Beat the Paper

Before asking which scientist is best, it is worth knowing whether any of them do real work. They do. Figure 35 shows the distribution of held-out improvement over the paper’s source method, one panel per mode. Most runs land to the right of zero: 84% beat the reproduced method when improving it, and 74% do when designing a new one from scratch. Innovate carries the heavier left tail, since a fresh design more often fails outright, yet even there the typical attempt still moves the metric forward.

F.2 Do the Gains Generalize

A score is only meaningful if it reflects a real gain rather than a metric gamed during the run. The held-out split separates the two: a scientist optimizes against a training-phase metric but is scored on a test slice it never sees. Figure 36 plots one against the other. The two track closely (Spearman 0.570.57 in improve and 0.690.69 in innovate), so training gains usually survive to the held-out metric, and only a small share of runs fall in the overfit quadrant where a training gain reverses on test (8% in improve and 5% in innovate). The split rarely needs to intervene, but when it does it removes exactly the runs that would otherwise inflate a score.

F.3 Effort and Outcomes

A natural worry is that a score mostly tracks how much compute or interaction a run spent, rewarding brute force over insight. It does not. Figure 37 plots each run’s within-paper normalized score against the GPU-hours it consumed and the number of turns it took, with the Improve and Innovate modes kept apart. Every trend is flat: the rank correlation stays weak throughout and is slightly negative where it moves at all, at most 0.220.22 in magnitude. Spending more does not produce a better result; a better method does.

Appendix G Experimental Setup

This section records the concrete setup behind our experiments: the paper set the scientists attempt, the compute pool they run on, the agent scaffolds and models we compare, and how trials are run and scored.

G.1 Data

All papers come from arXiv. We work from a global index of 124,816 unique papers in the categories cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.AI, and cs.LG, built from daily listings between January 1, 2025 and March 1, 2026 and exported on March 28, 2026. From this index, the selection procedure of §D chooses a category-balanced set of 1,000 papers to attempt; the per-stage counts are reported there.

G.2 Compute

’s experiments run on a heterogeneous setup provisioned through Hive and accounted by Nexus. The compute pool contains 16 A100 GPU nodes, 16 H100 GPU nodes, 16 H200 GPU nodes, and 4 CPU nodes (Table 13). The GPU nodes support accelerator-heavy reproduction jobs, while the CPU nodes support CPU-only experiments and non-accelerated setup or validation work.

G.3 Agent Scaffolds

Each scientist reaches the workspace through a scaffold, the layer that drives a coding-agent command-line tool behind one uniform turn interface (§A.4). Our experiments center on two scaffolds: Claude Code, which runs Anthropic models, and Codex, which runs OpenAI models. The same harness also supports other agents, including Gemini, Kimi, and Grok, so a single task can be run across a range of models. We prioritize a provider’s official agent scaffold when one is released; otherwise we use Claude Code as the default. Because a model and its scaffold are evaluated together and not every model runs through the same scaffold, the unit being compared is a model together with its scaffold, and a scaffold difference is part of what the comparison measures rather than something controlled away.

G.4 Models

We evaluate scientists built on models from seven providers: Anthropic (Fable 5.1, Fable 5, Opus 4.8, and Opus 4.7), OpenAI (GPT 6 Astra, GPT 5.6 Sol, GPT 5.5, and GPT 5.4), Zhipu (GLM 5.2 and GLM 5.1), Moonshot (Kimi K2.7 and Kimi K2.6), MiniMax (MiniMax M3 and MiniMax M2.7), Xiaomi (MiMo V2.5 Pro), and DeepSeek (DeepSeek V4). Anthropic and OpenAI models run through their official scaffolds; the rest run through Claude Code against an Anthropic-compatible gateway (§G.3). Every model is run at the extra-high (xhigh) reasoning-effort setting, or at its highest available setting if it does not support xhigh, so models are judged at full strength rather than at a throttled setting.

G.5 Evaluation Trials

Every trial hands the scientist the same resources, so a difference in outcome reflects the model and not the budget behind it. A trial runs under a ceiling of 200 turns and a compute budget of 30 GPU-hours, with at most 2 GPUs held at once, accounted by Nexus (§A.2). A trial that aborts for a transient infrastructure reason, such as a gateway timeout or a compute-pool blip, is retried up to three times before it is recorded as a failure; retries cover infrastructure, never an agent that simply solved the task poorly, so no model is re-run for doing badly. We cap in-flight trials at 30 and split that capacity evenly across the active models, so a fast API does not crowd a slower one out of the queue. Each model is run in both evaluation modes of §E.1. GPU-hours are counted as wall-clock time times the number of GPUs held, without weighting by accelerator class, so a trial scheduled onto faster cards can fit more experimentation into the same nominal budget; we treat this as a known limitation of expressing the budget in raw GPU-hours.

G.6 Provider Failures

A run spans thousands of unattended turns over hours or days, during which a model provider can rate-limit, throttle, or go down. The two settings absorb these interruptions differently, because they optimize for different things. When building an environment, the goal is to preserve work, so a run that fails resumes from the start of the current workflow iteration, reusing the saved workspace; a provider outage then costs at most the iteration in progress, not the whole reproduction. During evaluation, the goal is fairness, so a trial that fails before producing any score is discarded and restarted from a fresh workspace rather than resumed: no model is scored on a run that was continued mid-trajectory or warm-started from partial state, and every model meets the same clean-room conditions. A failure that occurs after scores are written is set aside for review rather than silently retried.

G.7 Cohort and Normalization

Running every model on all 1,000 selected papers would be expensive to repeat, so the headline evaluation uses a smaller fixed cohort drawn from the lower-compute environments, chosen so that a full pass stays cheap enough to run across many models and to rerun over time. Scores are normalized against a reference set of models rather than reported in absolute terms (§E.3): the per-paper normalization coefficients are computed once from that reference set and then frozen, so a newly added model is scored against the existing board without shifting the numbers already reported for other models. The reference set is the current generation of each model family; older generations are scored against that frozen reference but kept out of it.

G.8 Reproducibility

Every trial starts from the same pinned container image and the same workspace template (§C), so the software environment and the starting state are identical across models and stay fixed as the evaluation is rerun over months. Scoring depends only on the numbers a trial records, not on wall-clock time or the hardware it ran on (§B.2), so a trial can be rescored later without rerunning the agent. We retain the full record of each trial, the agent log, the final workspace, and the jobs it submitted, so any reported score can be traced back to what the agent actually did.

Appendix H Dataset and Training Details

This appendix documents the two artifacts behind §4: the released trace corpus (§4.2) and the scientist trained on it (§4.3). It records how the corpus is counted, how the training data and configuration are derived from it, and the held-out protocol behind Figure 15.

H.1 Trace Corpus

What Is Preserved.

Every evaluation attempt is preserved as its own git repository, one per environment, model, and run mode. The repository is the final workspace of §C with its full commit history: the system commits after every turn (§C.4), so the corpus holds the development history of each attempt rather than a cleaned final state. A trace records the research idea and its revisions, the method code as it changed, and the per-experiment logs and scores, tied together by the turn-by-turn trajectory that produced them. Attempts that regress on the source method are kept alongside those that improve on it; a corpus of research being done must include the failures.

Accounting.

The totals in §4.2 are computed per attempt and summed. Hours of work is the scientist’s end-to-end running wall-clock time, from the first turn of a trial to its final recorded score; summed over every preserved attempt, across all models, effort tiers, and both modes, it gives the roughly 6,400 hours reported. The per-attempt averages of Table 4 come from the same records.

H.2 Training Data

Provenance.

All training data derives from finished evaluation traces. Each example is rooted in a task specification exactly as a scientist receives it: the problem, the constraints, and the metric to move (§C). The ten held-out papers of §H.4 appear in no training example.

Supervised Set.

The SFT set has 1,000 examples. The prompt is the task specification; the target is the attempt’s reasoning inside <think> tags followed by its final idea. Reasoning is cleaned before training: fabricated run results and job identifiers are removed, and empirical claims are reframed as conceptual, with nothing invented or added. The set combines 925 authentic completions with 75 faithful rephrasings of the strongest completions, which round the set to 1,000 without introducing new content.

Reward Set.

The GRPO set has 1,500 already-scored ideas, rewarded by measured outcomes only: 777 examples by the held-out test score (weight 1.0), and 723 by generalization, the test score minus the train-test overfit gap (weight 0.5). Rewards are z-normalized within each paper and mode group, so an idea is reinforced or suppressed relative to the other ideas for the same task. We deliberately exclude rewards judged by an LLM: every reward in the set is a measured result.

H.3 Training Procedure

Setup.

The base model is Qwen3-8B in its thinking variant. Both stages train a LoRA adapter of rank 32 through Tinker (Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), and the GRPO stage continues from the SFT checkpoint.

SFT.

Cross-entropy on the assistant message only, learning rate 10−410^{-4}, batch size 8, 3 epochs, maximum sequence length 8,192. Training NLL decreases from 2.25 to 2.16 over the three epochs.

Offline GRPO.

The objective is a clipped PPO loss. The SFT policy’s log-probabilities are computed with a no-gradient forward pass and used as the reference, so the clip bounds every update to a trust region around the SFT policy. Learning rate 10−510^{-5}, batch size 16, one epoch, gradient-norm clip 1.0. Training stays bounded: the completion NLL oscillates in a stable band around the SFT baseline and never diverges. This stability is not free. An earlier variant that weighted cross-entropy by the signed advantage collapsed, because tokens with negative advantage are pushed toward unboundedly low log-probability; the clipped objective with an explicit reference policy is what makes offline training on scored ideas stable.

H.4 Held-Out Evaluation

Protocol.

The gym result of Figure 15 scores ideas, not the idea generator’s own coding. For each of the ten held-out papers, one idea is sampled from each of the three checkpoints, base, SFT, and GRPO, with the same prompt format, temperature 0.7, and top-p 0.8. A single fixed implementer, GPT 5.6 Sol at the xhigh effort tier, then executes every idea in innovate mode under identical conditions: the idea is injected into the briefing with the instruction to implement it faithfully and to optimize within its framing rather than invent a different approach. Only the idea’s origin varies across the thirty runs.

Scoring and Isolation.

Scoring is identical to the benchmark: the held-out FNI, computed with each paper’s frozen cohort coefficients (§G.7). The ablation is isolated from the leaderboard: it runs in a separate workspace namespace, shifts no normalization, and publishes nothing.

Results.

Figure 38 plots each trained idea’s score against the same paper’s base idea score, and Table 14 summarizes the distributions over the ten held-out papers. Both the mean and the median rise monotonically from base to SFT to GRPO. The spread grows as well, so the gain is a shift in the typical outcome rather than a uniform improvement on every paper.

Appendix I Example Produced Environment

This section uses one finished environment as a lens on what the builders actually do, and why. For each choice a builder makes while turning a paper into a reusable task, we ask why it makes that choice and whether the behavior is one the system is built to elicit or the builder’s own judgment. The paper is only background: it is the reproduction of Transformers without Normalization (arXiv:2503.10622), whose Dynamic Tanh (DyT) replaces Layer Normalization with a learnable element-wise operation. The run used MiniMax M2.7, GLM 5.1, and GPT 5.4 across 25 agent sessions over the reproduce, design, package, and verify roles, and about 19 GPU-hours, ending at the core_claim milestone. The few excerpts below come from the produced workspace; layout follows Figure 25.

Implement the real method, not a lookalike.

The reproducer writes the paper’s actual computation rather than a model tuned to emit its published numbers. It does this because the milestone rewards a method that runs: a surrogate fit to the reported accuracy would clear a naive number-matching test but fails ours by construction, and the verifier re-checks that the code is the algorithm itself. This is designed in — the milestone ladder and the verify role reward a runnable method (§A.3).

⬇
def forward(self, x): # DyT(x) = gamma * tanh(alpha*x) + beta
return self.gamma * torch.tanh(self.alpha * x) + self.beta
def replace_ln_with_dyt(model, init_alpha=0.5):
for name, m in list(model.named_modules()):
if isinstance(m, (nn.LayerNorm, nn.RMSNorm)): # swap every norm layer
set_submodule(model, name, DyT(m.normalized_shape[-1], init_alpha))
return model
Write the briefing so it cannot leak the answer.

The builder states the problem in method-agnostic terms: it fixes the question and the success criteria but never names DyT or normalization-free training. Why withhold what it just implemented? Because the same workspace is later handed to a from-scratch scientist, and a brief that named the solution would let that scientist copy it instead of doing research. By design, briefings must be method-agnostic, and the verifier and validate.py flag leaks; one is caught below.

⬇
## Research Question
Can deep transformer-style classifiers be trained stably and accurately when
their usual feature-normalization components are removed or replaced, without
winning by increasing model size, changing the data, or using pretrained weights?
## Success Criteria
- Train without numerical divergence; match or improve the reference accuracy.
- Keep parameter count and model scale matched within the comparison.
- Same data split and preprocessing; no pretrained weights, extra data, or ensembles.
Decide what counts as an improvement.

The scoring contract is where the builder exercises judgment the system asks for but does not dictate. It makes top-1 accuracy the primary metric, keeps top-5 and balanced accuracy as diagnostics, and gives parameter count a negative coefficient — so beating the baseline by scaling the model up does not register as a win. The format invites such a constraint metric; which metrics matter, and by how much, is the builder’s call. It records the paper’s reported numbers as the ranking reference and its own measured numbers as the baseline a future method must beat.

Scale the experiment down without trivializing it.

The full paper trains ViT-B/L for 300 epochs, beyond a per-paper budget, so the builder scales to a 50-class slice and a ViT-S/16. The choice is bounded by a rule the system cares about: model and data scale may shrink, but the algorithm and the matched comparison must be preserved, and the task must stay hard enough to discriminate. The builder checks this — the LayerNorm baseline lands below saturation, so comparison still has room, and DyT edges it at equal parameter count.

Pin the surface a future scientist competes on.

Because the environment is graded by comparison, the builder writes down what a future scientist may optimize, what it must hold fixed, and where it may explore. It splits this into three documents: a target (what improvement means and how it is measured), constraints (what must stay matched across compared systems), and a direction (the mechanism to work on, and what is out of bounds). These are required and method-safe: a from-scratch reader sees the rules, not the solution.

⬇
## Primary: supervised_classification
Improve accuracy on the matched ImageNet class slice without increasing model
scale or changing the data.
- Benefit: top1_accuracy (top5_accuracy, balanced_accuracy as diagnostics)
- Constraint: param_count_M within 5% of the matched reference
- Success: top-1 within 1 pt of the reference, with no parameter increase
⬇
## Model Scale
Candidate and reference must have matched scale: param_count_M within 5%.
A larger candidate is an extra experiment, not an improvement.
## Training Budget
Same data, epoch budget, optimizer, augmentation, and preprocessing. A recipe
change counts only when it is applied to every system in the comparison.
⬇
## Direction Scope
Work on normalization as a mechanism: stabilize activations, gradients, or
optimization while keeping the compared architecture and data fixed.
## Out of Bounds
- Resource scaling as the only change - Pretrained weights or extra data
- Ensembles - Switching to an easier or different dataset
Keep evaluation independent of any one method.

The builder makes the evaluator score prediction files and own the labels, rather than load the reproduced model. Why give up the convenience of calling its own checkpoint? Because a future method, however different from DyT, must score through the same interface; an evaluator coupled to this run’s model would break for everyone else. The boundary is designed — and, as the next step shows, enforced rather than assumed.

Build a held-out test, and say where it is weak.

The designer adds a hidden test slice so a later scientist cannot quietly overfit the visible scores, and — notably — writes down why it chose this split and where it falls short. The choice of split is the builder’s own judgment; that it records the trade-off is the behavior the design-notes step is meant to produce.

⬇
### Split style: per-class alternating validation parity
Within each class, even-position images go to train and odd-position to test.
Why this fits: both slices have comparable difficulty, so an honest method
scores similarly on both, while a method that games the visible slice shows a gap.
Known limitation: the parity split is moderate. A harder split (held-out classes
or OOD) gives a stronger shortcut signal but needs a larger dataset.
Catch the system’s own mistakes.

The last role is where design meets behavior. The verifier audited the artifact and found that an earlier builder had let the evaluator load the reproduced checkpoint — a method leak that would silently break from-scratch mode. It moved inference into method/ and rewrote eval/ as a generic prediction-file scorer. The system is built to catch exactly this class of error (the verify role together with validate.py), and here it did.

⬇
## Issues found
- Critical, fixed: eval/ contained solution-specific checkpoint loading. Even
without importing from method/, this leaked the reproduced algorithm into the
reusable evaluation path and would compromise from-scratch mode.
## Fixes applied
- Moved checkpoint inference into method/; rewrote eval/ as a generic evaluator
that scores JSONL predictions from any method without knowing the algorithm.

Only after this check passed did the workspace settle at core_claim. Every choice above is committed: the run writes a manifest.json and a README.md reproduction log, and the git history checkpoints each turn, so each decision traces back to the builder, the jobs, and the code behind it (§C).
